READING PASSAGE 1: The Last Drying Rack
For forty years, the print studio had dried paper on wooden racks that descended from the ceiling like narrow ladders. Lina knew each rack by its noises. Rack Three sighed when lowered. Rack Seven stopped two centimeters above the floor unless someone nudged its rope. The newest volunteers complained, reasonably, that the racks were awkward and slow.

A grant allowed the studio to buy rolling metal screens. They were clean, bright, and easy to rearrange. During installation, Lina labeled the old racks for removal. She felt no ceremony; equipment either served the work or it did not. Still, she postponed taking down Rack Seven because a class was using the wall beneath it.

That afternoon, a student named Dev printed a broad field of dark ink around a small unprinted circle. He had pressed too hard, and the paper carried a shallow ridge. On a flat screen the wet sheet sagged, allowing ink to pool along the ridge. Dev reached for another sheet, but Lina stopped him. She clipped the print to Rack Seven so that it hung vertically. Gravity drew the extra ink downward in thin, even paths. The mistake became a ring of lines around the white circle.

Dev asked whether the rack was designed for that effect. Lina nearly said yes. Instead, she explained that printers had long improvised with whatever the studio provided. The rack’s spacing, worn clips, and vertical drop could all leave marks. Most were flaws; a few became choices once the printer noticed them.

The next morning, Lina removed six old racks. She kept Rack Seven, but not as a monument. She mounted it lower, replaced its rope, and placed a card beside it: “Vertical drying rack. Slower than screens. Useful when gravity is part of the print.” Dev added a smaller handwritten note: “Ask the paper what falling can do.”

The studio looked larger with the other racks gone. The metal screens rolled neatly against one wall. Rack Seven no longer sighed or stuck. It remained because Lina had finally described its use precisely, not because she had refused to change.

Lina asked the next class to test the rack rather than accept the card as a rule. Students hung narrow test strips at different angles and used ink of two viscosities. Most combinations produced nothing worth keeping: blunt drips, pale edges, or paper that curled. A few created lines that could be repeated if clip position and ink thickness were recorded. Dev entered those conditions in a shared notebook.

The test did not make the rack indispensable. A future printer might find no reason to use it, and the studio could remove it when space changed again. For now, however, it occupied a defined place among the tools. The metal screens offered speed and consistency; the rack offered a controlled way to let motion continue after printing. Lina considered that distinction a better form of preservation than simply refusing to take old equipment down.

At the end of the term, Dev made two editions of the same image. One dried flat and retained a smooth black field; the other hung from Rack Seven and carried thin descending lines. He displayed them side by side without naming one correct and the other accidental. The difference lay in whether he had anticipated the movement and prepared the ink for it. Lina saw that the surviving rack had acquired a clearer purpose through the comparison. Its age had prompted the question, but a repeatable result—not age—had earned it space in the studio.

Other volunteers began applying the same rule to equipment stored elsewhere in the building. A heavy paper cutter remained because its alignment was unusually accurate; a cracked tray was photographed and discarded because no one could name a use that justified its leak. The conversations were sometimes difficult, but they replaced the broad categories of “old” and “new” with narrower questions about effect, safety, and repetition. Rack Seven had not won an exemption. It had helped the studio develop a better standard for change.

Which statement best explains the significance of the passage’s ending?
A) The ending or visual contradicts every claim made earlier in the passage.
B) The final section introduces a new subject that has no connection to the passage.
C) The evidence establishes a universal rule with no exceptions or limitations.
D) Dev’s handwritten note extends Lina’s practical label by expressing the same discovery in imaginative language.

options.A: The ending or visual contradicts every claim made earlier in the passage.
options.B: The final section introduces a new subject that has no connection to the passage.
options.C: The evidence establishes a universal rule with no exceptions or limitations.
options.D: Dev’s handwritten note extends Lina’s practical label by expressing the same discovery in imaginative language.

questions.explanation: The correct choice integrates the ending or visual with the passage’s central development.

questions.stem:
READING PASSAGE 2: Restoring Kelp by Sound
A healthy kelp forest is not silent. Water moves through fronds, fish scrape algae from rocks, and invertebrates produce clicks and snaps. To a diver, many of these sounds blur into a faint crackle. To the larvae of some marine animals, however, the soundscape may provide information about where to settle.

This possibility has led restoration researchers to test underwater speakers near damaged reefs. A speaker plays recordings from a thriving habitat, and scientists compare the animals arriving near that speaker with those arriving near a silent control. In several studies, more juvenile fish appeared near the playback. The result suggests that sound can influence movement, but it does not show that every arriving animal will remain or that the habitat can support it.

Kelp restoration makes this limitation especially important. Young fish may be attracted to a recording, yet they still need shelter and food. If heat, pollution, or grazing has removed the kelp, sound alone cannot rebuild the physical habitat. Researchers therefore pair acoustic playback with other actions, such as planting juvenile kelp or reducing the number of grazing sea urchins.

The recordings themselves also require care. A reef varies by season and time of day. Boat engines can mask biological sounds, and a recording made close to one noisy species may not represent the habitat as a whole. Teams use several microphones, remove obvious equipment noise, and report the volume at which a recording is played. Excessive volume could attract animals from an unrealistically large area or disturb species the project intends to help.

Acoustic playback is best understood as one tool for testing and guiding recovery. If fish approach a restored plot more often when an appropriate soundscape is present, researchers can investigate whether the newcomers feed, grow, and remain. The method turns sound into a measurable part of habitat quality while keeping the larger requirement in view: a convincing invitation matters only if there is somewhere suitable to stay.

A long-term trial therefore follows more than arrival counts. Divers survey fish size and feeding behavior, cameras record how long individuals remain, and kelp measurements track canopy growth. Researchers may turn the speakers off after several weeks to learn whether any effect persists. If fish leave immediately, the sound may have acted only as a temporary cue. If they stay and use the restored habitat, playback may have helped a recovering community cross an early threshold.

The control sites are equally important. Natural recruitment can change from month to month, and a regional increase could make every plot look successful. Comparing silent and playback plots exposed to the same broader conditions helps separate that background variation from the effect of sound. The design does not make the ecosystem simple; it makes one proposed contribution testable.

The same caution applies when results are communicated to the public. A headline that says “sound restores reefs” compresses several uncertain steps into one claim. A more accurate description separates attraction, settlement, survival, and reproduction. Each can be measured on a different schedule and may respond to a different feature of the habitat. Researchers welcome interest in an unusual tool, but they also publish silent controls and unsuccessful trials. Those results reveal where playback stops being effective and where conventional restoration—water quality, grazing control, and kelp establishment—must do the essential work.

Site selection further complicates the work. A recording from a healthy forest may contain species that cannot live at the damaged site because depth, temperature, or current differs. Researchers therefore compare the source and restoration site before choosing a soundscape, and they may build a composite from several periods rather than loop one dramatic minute. The goal is not to make the site sound generically lively. It is to test cues that plausibly belong to the habitat the project is capable of supporting.

Which statement best explains the significance of the passage’s ending?
F) The invitation metaphor emphasizes that sound may guide animals, whereas habitat conditions determine whether they can remain.
G) The ending or visual contradicts every claim made earlier in the passage.
H) The final section introduces a new subject that has no connection to the passage.
J) The evidence establishes a universal rule with no exceptions or limitations.

options.B: The ending or visual contradicts every claim made earlier in the passage.
options.C: The final section introduces a new subject that has no connection to the passage.
options.D: The evidence establishes a universal rule with no exceptions or limitations.

questions.stem:
PASSAGE A
Lena coordinated a school greenhouse that allowed residents to borrow specialized materials. At first, Lena assumed that adding more items would increase use. A short survey, however, showed that many visitors were uncertain about how to begin. The survey became a compass: it pointed the team toward clearer labels and a one-page guide. During the next month, completed loans rose from 22 to 31. Lena concluded that the collection had not needed to become larger; it had needed to become easier to navigate.

PASSAGE B
A second coordinator, Eli, agreed that instructions matter but argued that conversation is equally important. At Eli's site, volunteers greet new visitors and demonstrate one tool before explaining the catalog. Eli views the catalog as a reference, not a substitute for human guidance.

TABLE: Completed loans
Before revision: 22
After revision: 31

Which choice most accurately summarizes Passage A?
A) A team used survey results to improve access, and use increased afterward.
B) A team proved that labels always solve every community problem.
C) A collection failed because it had too many volunteers.
D) A survey showed that residents disliked borrowing materials.

options.A: A team used survey results to improve access, and use increased afterward.
options.B: A team proved that labels always solve every community problem.
options.C: A collection failed because it had too many volunteers.
options.D: A survey showed that residents disliked borrowing materials.

questions.explanation: The keyed response follows the text and targets 选择准确、无过度推断的概括.
